# A fracture alert in the emergency department {#sec-b09}

```{r}
#| label: setup-b09
#| include: false
source("../R/style.R")
set.seed(909)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** What does an alert mean when the prevalence changes?\
**For:** clinicians, medical students and reviewers who have to act on a positive image-analysis alert; the core
reading needs no programming. · **Prerequisites:** the fourfold table from @sec-b06; the idea of a target population
from @sec-b01.\
**In the course:** [W3 · Diagnostics, prediction and external
evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html)
· **Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b09-case}

It is the middle of a night shift in a fictitious emergency department. A junior doctor has just looked at the wrist
radiograph of a 67-year-old patient who fell on an outstretched hand. She sees no fracture. The image-analysis tool
that the department is piloting has placed a box over the distal radius with the label "possible fracture – second
look recommended". The information sheet states a sensitivity and specificity of 90% each; in this chapter both values
are *assumptions*. The doctor now has to choose: call the on-call senior to review the image, splint the wrist and book
a follow-up radiograph, or discharge the patient with advice. Before she decides, she asks the question this chapter
answers: how often is a box like this one right? The answer depends less on the tool than on who comes through the
door.

## Core reading {#sec-b09-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W3 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

```{r}
#| label: b09-core-numbers
#| echo: false
# The same numbers are recomputed step by step in the lab; here they feed the text and the table.
n_examined <- 1000
prev <- c(A = 0.05, B = 0.20)
se <- 0.90
sp <- 0.90
frac <- n_examined * prev
tp <- round(se * frac)
fn <- frac - tp
no_frac <- n_examined - frac
fp <- round((1 - sp) * no_frac)
tn <- no_frac - fp
alerts <- tp + fp
ppv <- tp / alerts
npv <- tn / (tn + fn)
shifts <- 90 # assumption: 1,000 examinations over 30 days with three shifts per day
```

**Two settings, one tool.** We compare two hypothetical care settings. In setting A, an emergency department
radiographs every patient with a limb injury; 5% of the patients examined actually have a fracture. In setting B,
patients are referred from a trauma clinic because a clinician already suspects a fracture; here 20% have one. Each
setting examines 1,000 patients. For this calculation we give the tool the same sensitivity (the share of fractures
that it flags) and the same specificity (the share of patients without fracture that it leaves unflagged) in both
settings: 90% each. This is of the same order as pooled estimates from a meta-analysis of AI fracture detection, in
which about half of the included studies had a high risk of bias [@kuo2022fracture; *published*]. **The key
assumption is that sensitivity and specificity do not change between the two settings.** In practice this assumption often fails, because the mix of injuries, patients and imaging differs between settings.
A meta-epidemiological study of 23 diagnostic meta-analyses found that sensitivity or specificity often varied with
prevalence; specificity tended to be lower where prevalence was higher [@leeflang2013prevalence; *published*]. Any
real deployment would therefore have to measure both values locally.

**Absolute numbers first.** Before any percentage, count people. In setting A, 50 of the 1,000 patients have a
fracture. The tool flags 45 of them and misses 5. Of the 950 patients without a fracture, the tool flags 95 and leaves
855 unflagged. In setting B, 200 patients have a fracture: 180 are flagged and 20 are missed. Of the 800 without a
fracture, 80 are flagged and 720 are not. Counts of this kind, called natural frequencies, are easier to reason with
than conditional probabilities [@hoffrage2000frequencies]. @tbl-b09-fourfold shows them as two fourfold tables and
@fig-b09-icons shows every patient as one symbol.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b09-fourfold
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Fourfold tables for 1,000 patients examined in each setting. Sensitivity and specificity of 90% are assumptions; all counts are synthetic. Independent unit: patient (n = 1,000 per setting)."
four <- data.frame(
  setting = rep(c("A · 5% prevalence", "B · 20% prevalence"), each = 2),
  tool = rep(c("alert", "no alert"), times = 2),
  fracture = c(tp[1], fn[1], tp[2], fn[2]),
  no_fracture = c(fp[1], tn[1], fp[2], tn[2])
)
four$total <- four$fracture + four$no_fracture
four$share_with_fracture <- paste0(four$fracture, "/", four$total, " = ",
                                   cdsr_percent(four$fracture / four$total))
knitr::kable(four, format = "pipe", align = "llrrrr",
             col.names = c("Setting", "Tool output", "Fracture", "No fracture", "Total",
                           "Share with fracture"))
```

**Then the denominator.** The positive predictive value (PPV) answers the junior doctor's question: of all patients
with an alert, how many have a fracture? Its denominator is every patient with an alert, not every patient with a
fracture. In setting A, `r alerts[1]` patients receive an alert and `r tp[1]` of them have a fracture: the PPV is
`r tp[1]`/`r alerts[1]` = `r cdsr_percent(ppv[1])`. In setting B the same tool gives `r tp[2]`/`r alerts[2]` =
`r cdsr_percent(ppv[2])`. Nothing about the software has changed; only the patients have. The negative predictive
value (NPV) moves in the other direction, from `r cdsr_percent(npv[1])` in A to `r cdsr_percent(npv[2])` in B. A
missing alert is therefore not an all-clear: in B, `r fn[2]` of 1,000 patients have a fracture that the tool did not
flag. The general relationship between prevalence and predictive values is worked through in [Methods in R:
Predictive Values and
Prevalence](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-predictive-values-prevalence)
and in the CTTIR lab [Diagnostic testing: Se, Sp, PPV, NPV,
LR](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course1_foundations/labs/lab_week2_session3.html) [@altman1994predictive].

```{r}
#| label: fig-b09-icons
#| fig-cap: "Every symbol is one of 1,000 patients examined per setting, ordered by tool output and reference result. The alerts (first two blocks) form the denominator of the positive predictive value. Synthetic counts; sensitivity and specificity of 90% are assumptions. Independent unit: patient (n = 1,000 per setting)."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of 1,000 symbols each, arranged in 20 rows of 50. Panel A, 5% prevalence: 45 filled circles for alerts with a fracture, 95 filled squares for alerts without a fracture, 5 filled triangles for missed fractures and 855 small open grey circles for patients without fracture or alert. Panel B, 20% prevalence: 180 filled circles, 80 filled squares, 20 filled triangles and 720 small open grey circles. In panel A the squares outnumber the circles; in panel B the circles outnumber the squares."
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)
# One row per patient; categories in the order alert/fracture, alert/no fracture, missed, neither
categories <- c("Alert, fracture (true positive)", "Alert, no fracture (false positive)",
                "No alert, fracture (false negative)", "No alert, no fracture (true negative)")
icons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(i) {
  counts <- c(tp[i], fp[i], fn[i], tn[i])
  data.frame(
    setting = sprintf("%s · prevalence %s · PPV %d/%d = %s", names(prev)[i], cdsr_percent(prev[i], 0),
                      tp[i], alerts[i], cdsr_percent(ppv[i])),
    category = factor(rep(categories, times = counts), levels = categories),
    position = 0:(n_examined - 1)
  )
}))
icons$column <- icons$position %% 50
icons$row <- icons$position %/% 50
ggplot(icons, aes(column, -row, colour = category, shape = category, size = category)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ setting, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(c(cdsr_colours["blue"], cdsr_colours["red"],
                                        cdsr_colours["orange"], "grey70"))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 15, 17, 1)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(1.9, 1.9, 1.9, 0.9)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2), shape = guide_legend(ncol = 2), size = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL, size = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic data · n = 1,000 patients per setting · sensitivity = specificity = 90% (assumption)") +
  theme_cdsr() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

**Three research questions, not one.** The fourfold table invites a single verdict: "the tool works" or "it does not".
In fact three separate questions are at stake, and each needs its own design.

1. *Model performance.* How well does the tool separate patients with and without fracture, compared with a defined
   reference standard, in the population where it will be used? This is a diagnostic accuracy study, reported
   according to STARD-AI [@sounderajah2025stardai]. It yields sensitivity, specificity and predictive values with
   confidence intervals.
2. *Patient benefit.* Do patients whose images are assessed with the tool have fewer missed fractures with
   consequences, without more harm from extra imaging, immobilisation or waiting? Accuracy cannot answer this. It
   needs a comparison group and outcomes that matter to patients, for example in a cluster-randomised or
   stepped-wedge study.
3. *Organisational burden.* How many additional second looks does the tool create per shift, and who absorbs them?
   If 1,000 examinations fall into `r shifts` shifts (30 days with three shifts each; an *assumption*), setting A
   produces about `r cdsr_number(alerts[1] / shifts, 1)` alerts per shift, `r cdsr_number(fp[1] / shifts, 1)` of
   them false. Setting B produces `r cdsr_number(alerts[2] / shifts, 1)` alerts per shift, of which
   `r cdsr_number(fp[2] / shifts, 1)` are false. Early clinical evaluations of this kind are reported along the lines
   of DECIDE-AI [@vasey2022decideai].

**Reader study and local pilot answer different questions.** In a reader study, several clinicians read the same set of
images with and without the tool. Such a study can show whether the tool changes readers' accuracy under controlled
conditions. Its case mix is usually chosen by design: in one multi-reader study of fracture detection on radiographs,
the fracture prevalence was fixed at 50% [@guermazi2022reader; *published*]. A PPV from such a set says little about
setting A. A local pilot, for example in silent mode, records how often the tool alerts in the department's own case
mix, what the local PPV is and how long second looks take. Neither design on its own shows that patients are better
off.

**A lower PPV alone is no reason to reject a product.** Setting A's PPV of `r cdsr_percent(ppv[1])` sounds poor. Whether
it is acceptable depends on what a false alert costs (a few minutes of a senior clinician's time, perhaps an extra
view) and on what a true alert gains. The gain is not `r tp[1]` detected fractures: it is the fractures among them that
the clinicians would otherwise have missed. Weighing these consequences is a decision analysis, not a property of the
PPV [@vickers2006dca]; @sec-b06 develops it with thresholds and net benefit.

**Saying it at handover.** A spoken handover in setting A could be: *"The tool has flagged the distal radius. In a
patient group like ours, only about one in three of these flags turns out to be a real fracture, so I would like a
second pair of eyes on the image before we decide."* In real operation, the "one in three" has to come from local
data, not from this exercise. The patient may then ask: *"If the computer is wrong two times out of three, why listen
to it at all, and would no box have meant that I could go home?"* A good answer explains that the box asks for a second
look but does not decide, and that a missing box lowers the probability of a fracture without ruling it out. The
clinical findings still count.

**Question for the workshop:** Your team works in setting A. Which single number would you put on the whiteboard for
the night shift – the PPV, the false alerts per shift or the missed fractures per month – and who should be told the
other two?

## Lab {#sec-b09-lab}

The lab recomputes every number from the core reading in base R, from the inputs to the predictive values. In W3, one
team works out setting A and another setting B by hand before anyone runs the code. Start a fresh R session in the
book folder. The following single line already reproduces both PPVs and is a useful first
check that R is running:

```{r}
#| label: b09-start
# Start command: PPV = true positives / all alerts, for 5% and 20% prevalence
round(100 * 0.9 * c(0.05, 0.20) / (0.9 * c(0.05, 0.20) + 0.1 * c(0.95, 0.80)), 1)
```

**Step 1 – inputs.** Each row describes one setting. Sensitivity and specificity are inputs, not results; in this
chapter they are assumptions.

```{r}
#| label: b09-inputs
cohorts <- data.frame(
  setting = c("A", "B"),
  description = c("unselected emergency department", "referred with clinical suspicion"),
  examined = c(1000L, 1000L),     # patients examined per setting
  prevalence = c(0.05, 0.20),     # share with fracture according to the reference standard
  sensitivity = c(0.90, 0.90),    # assumption: identical in both settings
  specificity = c(0.90, 0.90)     # assumption: identical in both settings
)
cohorts
```

**Step 2 – absolute frequencies.** People are counted in whole numbers, so every count is rounded explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: b09-counts
cohorts$fracture <- round(cohorts$examined * cohorts$prevalence)
cohorts$no_fracture <- cohorts$examined - cohorts$fracture
cohorts$true_pos <- round(cohorts$sensitivity * cohorts$fracture)        # alert and fracture
cohorts$false_neg <- cohorts$fracture - cohorts$true_pos                 # fracture without alert
cohorts$false_pos <- round((1 - cohorts$specificity) * cohorts$no_fracture) # alert without fracture
cohorts$true_neg <- cohorts$no_fracture - cohorts$false_pos              # neither
cohorts[, c("setting", "fracture", "true_pos", "false_neg", "no_fracture", "false_pos", "true_neg")]
```

**Step 3 – denominators and predictive values.** The alerts form the denominator of the PPV; the patients without an
alert form the denominator of the NPV.

```{r}
#| label: b09-ppv
cohorts$alerts <- cohorts$true_pos + cohorts$false_pos
cohorts$no_alerts <- cohorts$false_neg + cohorts$true_neg
cohorts$ppv <- cohorts$true_pos / cohorts$alerts
cohorts$npv <- cohorts$true_neg / cohorts$no_alerts
data.frame(setting = cohorts$setting,
           ppv = paste0(cohorts$true_pos, "/", cohorts$alerts, " = ", cdsr_percent(cohorts$ppv)),
           npv = paste0(cohorts$true_neg, "/", cohorts$no_alerts, " = ", cdsr_percent(cohorts$npv)))

# Target values from the core reading
stopifnot(
  cohorts$true_pos == c(45, 180),
  cohorts$false_pos == c(95, 80),
  cohorts$alerts == c(140, 260),
  isTRUE(all.equal(cohorts$ppv, c(45 / 140, 180 / 260))),
  cdsr_percent(cohorts$ppv) == c("32.1%", "69.2%"),
  # the lab and the hidden calculation behind the core reading agree
  cohorts$true_pos == tp, cohorts$false_pos == fp, cohorts$alerts == alerts
)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Sensitivity 90%" is often read as "90% of alerts are right". Sensitivity is conditioned on the fracture (45 of 50
fractures are flagged); the PPV is conditioned on the alert (45 of 140 alerts are fractures). Swapping the two
conditions turns 32.1% into 90% for the same 1,000 patients.
:::

**Step 4 – the workload per shift.** The number of shifts is an *assumption* and should be replaced by the local
rota. The calculation separates the alerts that need a second look from the false alerts among them.

```{r}
#| label: b09-shifts
shifts_per_1000 <- 90  # assumption: 30 days x 3 shifts for 1,000 examinations
cohorts$alerts_per_shift <- cohorts$alerts / shifts_per_1000
cohorts$false_alerts_per_shift <- cohorts$false_pos / shifts_per_1000
cohorts$missed_per_1000 <- cohorts$false_neg
cohorts[, c("setting", "alerts_per_shift", "false_alerts_per_shift", "missed_per_1000")]
stopifnot(round(cohorts$alerts_per_shift, 2) == c(1.56, 2.89))
```

Setting B produces more alerts per shift but fewer false ones: `r cohorts$false_pos[2]` against
`r cohorts$false_pos[1]` per 1,000 examinations. Workload and PPV are different quantities, and a team planning
staffing needs both.

**Step 5 – raw values for download.** The fourfold counts are stored as a small table so that W3 groups can start
from the file instead of the code.

```{r}
#| label: b09-save
raw <- cohorts[, c("setting", "description", "examined", "prevalence", "sensitivity", "specificity",
                   "true_pos", "false_pos", "false_neg", "true_neg")]
write.csv(raw, "../data/b09-fracture-alert-cohorts.csv", row.names = FALSE)
# Re-reading the file must give the same PPVs
check <- read.csv("../data/b09-fracture-alert-cohorts.csv")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(check$true_pos / (check$true_pos + check$false_pos), cohorts$ppv)))
```

The file [`data/b09-fracture-alert-cohorts.csv`](../data/b09-fracture-alert-cohorts.csv) contains only synthetic
counts and the two assumptions.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python with PyTorch"}
A fracture tool of this kind is usually a convolutional network trained on radiographs. The PyTorch tutorial on
[transfer learning](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/transfer_learning_tutorial.html) shows the standard
route: start from a ResNet-18 with ImageNet weights (`weights='IMAGENET1K_V1'`), resize to 256 pixels, crop to 224,
normalise with the ImageNet channel means and standard deviations and retrain the final layer
[@paszke2019pytorch]. The concrete advantage is access to pretrained weights and to research code that already works
on images; R would only consume the network's output. For a fair comparison with the counts in this chapter the
following must be identical and written down: the image set and the reference standard, the image orientation
(training with random horizontal flips mixes left and right), the conversion of greyscale radiographs to three
channels, the weights file and software version (torch 2.15.0 and torchvision 0.29.2 were current in November 2026),
and the threshold that turns a probability into an alert. Logit, probability and binary alert should be compared
separately. Patients often have two or three views; the counting unit for the fourfold table (patient or image) must
be the same on both sides. Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b09-countercheck}

Change one assumption and predict the direction before you compute. Suppose the department installs new radiography
equipment and the tool's specificity in setting A drops from 90% to 80%, while sensitivity stays at 90%. Does the PPV
halve, fall a little or stay the same? And what happens to the false alerts per shift?

```{r}
#| label: b09-countercheck
# Function: predictive values and counts for any combination of inputs
fourfold <- function(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, examined = 1000) {
  fracture <- round(examined * prevalence)
  true_pos <- round(sensitivity * fracture)
  false_pos <- round((1 - specificity) * (examined - fracture))
  data.frame(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, true_pos, false_pos,
             alerts = true_pos + false_pos, ppv = true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos))
}
changed <- rbind(fourfold(0.05, 0.90, 0.90), fourfold(0.05, 0.90, 0.80))
changed$false_alerts_per_shift <- changed$false_pos / shifts_per_1000
changed
stopifnot(changed$false_pos == c(95, 190), round(changed$ppv[2], 3) == 0.191)
```

The false alerts double, from 95 to 190 per 1,000 examinations, while the PPV falls from
`r cdsr_percent(changed$ppv[1])` to `r cdsr_percent(changed$ppv[2])`. At low prevalence, specificity drives the
workload. @fig-b09-ppv shows the same reasoning over a range of prevalences.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b09-ppv
#| fig-cap: "Positive predictive value as a function of fracture prevalence for sensitivity 90% and specificity 90% or 80% (assumptions). The two settings of the core reading are marked. Synthetic calculation; denominator: patients with an alert."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with prevalence from 1% to 40% on the horizontal axis and positive predictive value from 0% to 100% on the vertical axis. The solid line for specificity 90% rises steeply at low prevalence and passes through 32.1% at 5% prevalence (point A) and 69.2% at 20% prevalence (point B). The dashed line for specificity 80% lies below it at every prevalence, for example at about 19% for 5% prevalence."
#| code-fold: true
grid <- expand.grid(prevalence = seq(0.01, 0.40, by = 0.005), specificity = c(0.90, 0.80))
grid$ppv <- 0.90 * grid$prevalence / (0.90 * grid$prevalence + (1 - grid$specificity) * (1 - grid$prevalence))
grid$specificity <- factor(cdsr_percent(grid$specificity, 0), levels = c("90%", "80%"))
marks <- data.frame(prevalence = prev, ppv = ppv, label = paste0(names(prev), ": ", cdsr_percent(ppv)),
                    hjust = c(1.15, -0.15), vjust = c(-0.5, 1.3))  # label A above left, B below right
ggplot(grid, aes(prevalence, ppv, linetype = specificity, colour = specificity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(prevalence, ppv), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(prevalence, ppv, label = label, hjust = hjust, vjust = vjust),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) cdsr_percent(x, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) cdsr_percent(x, 0), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "red")])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = cdsr_linetypes[1:2]) +
  labs(x = "Fracture prevalence (share of patients examined)", y = "Positive predictive value",
       colour = "Specificity", linetype = "Specificity",
       caption = "Synthetic calculation · sensitivity 90% (assumption) · denominator: patients with an alert") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

A second counter-check changes the target population instead of the tool. If the tool were used for all radiographs
in a children's emergency department, which numbers in the table would you have to measure again before reusing any of
them? (All four cells: prevalence, injury pattern, image appearance and the reference standard can all differ.)

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b09-consequences}

**Ethics.** False alerts are not free. Patients may wait longer, receive an extra view or a CT scan with additional
radiation, or leave with a splint they did not need. Clinicians who see many uninformative alerts start to ignore
them: in one primary care study, acceptance of reminders fell with each additional reminder per encounter and with the
share of repeated reminders [@ancker2017alertfatigue; *published*]. The opposite risk is automation bias: a missing
box may be read as an all-clear. Who carries which share of these harms, and how uncertainty is explained to a patient,
is the subject of @sec-b21.

**Regulation.** The intended purpose decides the regulatory question, not the calculation. Software "intended to
provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" is classified at least as
class IIa under Rule 11 of Annex VIII of the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 [@eu2017mdr; binding text]. An AI
system that is itself a medical device and has to undergo third-party conformity assessment is a high-risk AI system
under Article 6(1) of the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 [@eu2024aiact; binding text]. Since the amending
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (published 24 July 2026, in force since 27 July 2026), the obligations of Chapter III,
Sections 1 to 3, apply to such systems from 2 August 2028 [@eu2026omnibus; binding text]. Whether the fictitious tool in this chapter is such a device, and who would be manufacturer and
who deployer, is examined in @sec-b22 by reading its intended purpose. Status: November 2026.

**Data protection.** The local pilot needs images, tool outputs and reference diagnoses. Whether an external service
provider needs the original images for this evaluation, or whether derived and minimised data suffice, is decided in
@sec-b23.

**Information security and operations.** If the tool fails or an unapproved model version is installed, reporting
must continue by the regular route without delay. @sec-b24 designs a failure test and that fallback; @sec-b20 uses
alerts per shift as a monitoring signal.

**The case returns four times.** In @sec-b21 a patient, a nurse and a researcher judge the same alert and the
distribution of false alerts. In @sec-b22 teams read the fictitious intended purpose. In @sec-b23 they decide whether a
service provider needs the original images. In @sec-b24 they design a failure test and a safe route back to regular
reporting.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b09-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** The manuscript reports a PPV of 70%. In which population was it measured, what was the
  prevalence, and was that prevalence fixed by the study design?
- **Self-test:** A smaller emergency department wants to use the tool only at night. It performs 400 limb radiographs
  per month on 30 night shifts. Assume a fracture prevalence of 10%, a sensitivity of 90% and, because of older
  equipment, a specificity of 80%. How many alerts and how many false alerts arise per night, what is the PPV, and
  should the department switch the tool off because the PPV is "only one third"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Of 400 patients, 40 have a fracture: 36 are flagged and 4 are missed. Of the 360 without a fracture, 72 are flagged
and 288 are not. There are 108 alerts, so the PPV is 36/108 = 33.3% and the NPV 288/292 = 98.6%. Per night shift this
means 3.6 alerts, 2.4 of them false. The PPV alone does not justify switching the tool off. The department needs to
know how long a second look takes at night, how many of the 36 flagged fractures the night team would otherwise have
missed, and whether the specificity of 80% reflects a local equipment problem that could be fixed. With
`fourfold(0.10, 0.90, 0.80, examined = 400)` the lab function reproduces these numbers.
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @leeflang2013prevalence supports the warning that sensitivity and specificity need not be transferable between
    settings with different prevalence.
  - @hoffrage2000frequencies is the reason why the chapter counts people before it computes percentages.
  - @altman1994predictive is the classic short explanation of predictive values and their dependence on prevalence.
  - @guermazi2022reader is the published example of a reader study with prevalence fixed by design.
  - @vickers2006dca introduces net benefit, the decision-analytic view behind "a lower PPV is not a verdict".
  - @ancker2017alertfatigue provides published evidence that more and repeated alerts are accepted less often.
  - @sounderajah2025stardai and @vasey2022decideai are the reporting guidelines for accuracy studies and early
    clinical evaluation.
  - @eu2017mdr, @eu2024aiact and @eu2026omnibus are the binding legal texts behind the regulatory paragraph.
